title: A Wound No One Will Heal
overview: Jeremiah warns that Judah's refusal to turn back from false gods and false comfort will bring invasion and ruin, and he grieves deeply over what is coming.

parts.label: Bones under the open sky (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Invaders would dig up graves, even those of kings and priests, and leave the bones lying before the sun, moon and stars that many in Judah had worshiped. The sky they served would simply look on, and survivors scattered to other lands would wish they had died.

parts.label: Why won't they turn back? (vv. 4-7)
parts.note: Jeremiah plays on the word "return": anyone who trips gets up, and anyone who takes a wrong turn goes back, yet the people keep charging ahead like a warhorse. Even migrating birds know when to come home, but the people do not know what God asks of them.

parts.label: False wisdom, false peace (vv. 8-13)
parts.note: The leaders boasted that they had God's law, but the scribes, the trained writers and teachers, had twisted it, though scholars are unsure whether this means bad copying, bad teaching or both. Priests and prophets treated a deep wound like a scratch, promising "peace" with disaster at the door, so homes, fields and harvests would be lost.

parts.label: Panic as the enemy comes (vv. 14-17)
parts.note: Now the people speak, deciding to run to walled towns only to die there, admitting their wrongs too late. Horses are heard from Dan, the far northern border where invaders entered, and the enemy is pictured as snakes no charmer can tame.

parts.label: A cry from far away (vv. 18-20)
parts.note: A grieving voice hears people asking whether the LORD has left Zion, though it is unclear whether these are exiles in a distant land or people at home dreading an enemy from far away. God breaks in to say their idols, not his absence, are the cause, and "the harvest is past" means season after season of hope has run out with no rescue.

parts.label: Is there no balm in Gilead? (vv. 21-22)
parts.note: The speaker feels the people's injury as his own. Gilead, east of the Jordan, was famous for a healing resin, so the cry asks why no cure has come; readers differ on whether this weeping voice is Jeremiah's, God's, or both.

think: When something in a life or a community is clearly going wrong, what makes it so hard to admit it and turn around?
